candidates.title: Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync Status: accepted, May 2025. ## Context Tidepool began as a personal library tool. Every design proposal that added a hosted component also added accounts, privacy questions, and ongoing costs. ## Decision Tidepool stores all data locally. There is no Tidepool account, no hosted sync service, and no telemetry. candidates.title: 2025-11 Sync storm
candidates.snippet: # 2025-11 Sync storm Date: November 2025. Severity: high. Owner: Jonas Weber. ## Summary A relay outage caused clients to retry aggressively. Retries amplified into a request storm when devices reconnected together, and some clients spun for hours. ## Timeline - Nov 3: relay rate limits began returning 429s. - Nov 4: retry storm; battery drain reports from users. - Nov 5: workaround published (disable relay sync); fix landed with exponential backoff and jitter. ## Root cause Retry logic had no backoff and no cap; reconnection was synchronized across devices. ## Follow-ups - Backoff and a retry budget shipped in v0.4.1. - Mobile clients were retired the following year (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]).

candidates.title: Decision - Drop the native mobile app
candidates.file_path: decisions/Decision - Drop the native mobile app.md
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Drop the native mobile app Status: accepted, August 2025. ## Context The two-person team maintained iOS and Android clients plus a relay service. Sync bugs on mobile consumed about half of each release cycle, and the relay added a server dependency the project did not want (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). ## Options considered 1. Keep both clients and hire: not viable for a volunteer team. 2. Keep one platform: still owned a relay and store review cycles. 3. Retire both and invest in the desktop engine: chosen. ## Decision Retire the native apps; keep a read-only web gallery for sharing. Direct users to the desktop import flow. ## Consequences - Mobile sync reliability issues end; community reaction was mixed. - The relay service was shut down in September 2025.

candidates.title: Sync Engine
candidates.snippet: # Sync Engine The sync engine moves a photo library between a user's devices without a server. Every device keeps a full local index; changes propagate as operation logs over the local network or through a user-provided shared folder. ## How it works - Each device runs a sync agent that watches the library directory for changes. - Operations are exchanged as append-only logs and applied through the conflict resolver (see [[Conflict Resolution]]). - Sync state lives in the same SQLite database as the library index (see [[Storage Layer]]). - Mobile clients used a different relay transport and were sunset in August 2025 (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]). ## Failure modes - A retry storm against a rate-limited relay caused the November 2025 incident (see [[2025-11 Sync storm]]). - Duplicate photo imports after v0.4.2 came from the dedup hash, not the engine (see [[2026-02 Duplicate photos after 0.4.2]]). ## Relations - relates_to [[Conflict Resolution]] - relates_to [[Storage Layer]] - relates_to [[Maya Chen]] - relates_to [[Jonas Weber]]

candidates.title: Conflict Resolution
candidates.snippet: # Conflict Resolution Conflicts happen when two devices edit the same library record before syncing. Tidepool resolves them deterministically so every device converges on the same state. ## Approach - Field-level last-writer-wins with hybrid logical clocks for metadata. - Photo membership and album edits use CRDT sets, adopted in January 2026 (see [[Decision - CRDT conflict resolution]]). - Deletions are tombstones, garbage-collected after 30 days without opposing edits. ## Why not simpler schemes - Server-authoritative resolution is off the table: Tidepool has no server (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). - Timestamp-only ordering broke across devices with skewed clocks. ## Relations - relates_to [[Sync Engine]] - relates_to [[Decision - CRDT conflict resolution]] - relates_to [[Maya Chen]]

candidates.title: Decision - SQLite over Postgres
candidates.snippet: # Decision - SQLite over Postgres Status: accepted, June 2025. ## Context The library index outgrew flat JSON files. Candidates were SQLite (embedded) and Postgres (server). ## Decision Use SQLite, one database per library. ## Rationale - Tidepool is single-user and local-first (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]); a server dependency contradicts the premise. - Backups are a file copy; no daemon, no ports, no credentials. - Full-text and vector search both work in-process, which keeps the sync engine simple. ## Consequences - Concurrent writers rely on WAL mode; multi-process access needs care. - Migrations run at startup and must stay backward compatible for one release.

candidates.title: Photo library format
candidates.snippet: # Photo library format A Tidepool library is one directory: library/ tidepool.db # index, metadata, sync state (SQLite) originals/ # content-addressed photo files cache/ # regenerable thumbnails ## Rules - Original files are immutable; file names are content hashes. - The content hash covers file bytes plus capture metadata, not the file path. - `cache/` may be deleted at any time; it rebuilds from originals. - Album and tag structure lives in the database, never in the file tree. See [[Decision - SQLite over Postgres]] and [[Decision - Progressive photo import]].

candidates.title: Storage Layer

candidates.title: Decision - CRDT conflict resolution
candidates.snippet: # Decision - CRDT conflict resolution Status: accepted, January 2026. ## Context Two devices editing the same album before syncing produced lost edits. Timestamp ordering failed across devices with skewed clocks; a server arbiter is impossible (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). ## Decision Use CRDTs for collaborative collections: - OR-Set for album membership and tags. - Hybrid logical clocks for scalar fields, last-writer-wins per field. - Tombstones for deletions, garbage-collected after 30 days. ## Alternatives rejected - Server arbitration: no server. - Manual conflict prompts: users found them confusing in beta. ## Consequences - Every client must upgrade together for full convergence. - Implemented in the sync engine behind a version flag (see [[Sync Engine]]).

candidates.title: Decision - Abandon the Electron wrapper
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Abandon the Electron wrapper Status: accepted, March 2026. ## Context The desktop shell wrapped the web UI in Electron. Bundle size, native module mismatches, and predictable security review noise kept costing release time. ## Decision Remove the Electron shell. Ship the local web UI as the primary desktop experience; revisit a native shell only if a concrete use case appears. ## Alternatives - Tauri: smaller, but a second toolchain to maintain for a two-person team. - Keep Electron: rejected on maintenance cost. ## Consequences - The installer shrinks; the auto-update path is temporarily manual. - Users who expected a dock icon get a documented browser-based flow.

candidates.title: Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync Status: accepted, May 2025. ## Context Tidepool began as a personal library tool. candidates.title: Sync Engine
candidates.snippet: # Sync Engine The sync engine moves a photo library between a user's devices without a server. Every device keeps a full local index; changes propagate as operation logs over the local network or through a user-provided shared folder. ## How it works - Each device runs a sync agent that watches the library directory for changes. - Operations are exchanged as append-only logs and applied through the conflict resolver (see [[Conflict Resolution]]). - Sync state lives in the same SQLite database as the library index (see [[Storage Layer]]). - Mobile clients used a different relay transport and were sunset in August 2025 (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]). ## Failure modes - A retry storm against a rate-limited relay caused the November 2025 incident (see [[2025-11 Sync storm]]). - Duplicate photo imports after v0.4.2 came from the dedup hash, not the engine (see [[2026-02 Duplicate photos after 0.4.2]]). ## Relations - relates_to [[Conflict Resolution]] - relates_to [[Storage Layer]] - relates_to [[Maya Chen]] - relates_to [[Jonas Weber]]

candidates.title: Storage Layer
candidates.snippet: # Storage Layer Each library is a single directory plus one SQLite database. The exact layout is specified in [[Photo library format]]. ## Design - SQLite holds the index, metadata, and sync state (see [[Decision - SQLite over Postgres]]). - Original files are never modified; thumbnails live in a regenerable cache. - Content hashes drive deduplication during import. - Import is chunked to keep memory flat on large libraries (see [[Decision - Progressive photo import]]). ## Known issues - The thumbnail cache was corrupted by a cache-invalidation bug in April 2026 (see [[2026-04 Corrupted thumbnail cache]]). - Jonas Weber owns this area. ## Relations - relates_to [[Jonas Weber]] - relates_to [[Decision - SQLite over Postgres]]

candidates.title: Decision - Progressive photo import
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Progressive photo import Status: accepted, October 2025. ## Context Importing a 200k-photo library in one pass held the whole manifest in memory and stalled the UI. ## Decision Stream imports in chunks of 500 files: hash, insert, and thumbnail each chunk, then release it. The manifest is a resumable journal (see [[Storage Layer]]). ## Consequences - Peak memory is flat regardless of library size. - Import can resume after a crash; partial imports are visible and repairable. - Progress reporting is chunk-granular rather than file-granular.

candidates.title: Photo library format
candidates.snippet: # Photo library format A Tidepool library is one directory: library/ tidepool.db # index, metadata, sync state (SQLite) originals/ # content-addressed photo files cache/ # regenerable thumbnails ## Rules - Original files are immutable; file names are content hashes. - The content hash covers file bytes plus capture metadata, not the file path. - `cache/` may be deleted at any time; it rebuilds from originals. - Album and tag structure lives in the database, never in the file tree. See [[Decision - SQLite over Postgres]] and [[Decision - Progressive photo import]].

candidates.title: Conflict Resolution
candidates.snippet: # Conflict Resolution Conflicts happen when two devices edit the same library record before syncing. Tidepool resolves them deterministically so every device converges on the same state. ## Approach - Field-level last-writer-wins with hybrid logical clocks for metadata. - Photo membership and album edits use CRDT sets, adopted in January 2026 (see [[Decision - CRDT conflict resolution]]). - Deletions are tombstones, garbage-collected after 30 days without opposing edits. ## Why not simpler schemes - Server-authoritative resolution is off the table: Tidepool has no server (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). - Timestamp-only ordering broke across devices with skewed clocks. ## Relations - relates_to [[Sync Engine]] - relates_to [[Decision - CRDT conflict resolution]] - relates_to [[Maya Chen]]

candidates.title: Decision - CRDT conflict resolution
candidates.snippet: # Decision - CRDT conflict resolution Status: accepted, January 2026. ## Context Two devices editing the same album before syncing produced lost edits. Timestamp ordering failed across devices with skewed clocks; a server arbiter is impossible (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). ## Decision Use CRDTs for collaborative collections: - OR-Set for album membership and tags. - Hybrid logical clocks for scalar fields, last-writer-wins per field. - Tombstones for deletions, garbage-collected after 30 days. ## Alternatives rejected - Server arbitration: no server. - Manual conflict prompts: users found them confusing in beta. ## Consequences - Every client must upgrade together for full convergence. - Implemented in the sync engine behind a version flag (see [[Sync Engine]]).

candidates.snippet: # Decision - SQLite over Postgres Status: accepted, June 2025. ## Context The library index outgrew flat JSON files. Candidates were SQLite (embedded) and Postgres (server). ## Decision Use SQLite, one database per library. ## Rationale - Tidepool is single-user and local-first (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]); a server dependency contradicts the premise. - Backups are a file copy; no daemon, no ports, no credentials. - Full-text and vector search both work in-process, which keeps the sync engine simple. ## Consequences - Concurrent writers rely on WAL mode; multi-process access needs care. - Migrations run at startup and must stay backward compatible for one release.

candidates.snippet: # Decision - Drop the native mobile app Status: accepted, August 2025. ## Context The two-person team maintained iOS and Android clients plus a relay service. Sync bugs on mobile consumed about half of each release cycle, and the relay added a server dependency the project did not want (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). ## Options considered 1. Keep both clients and hire: not viable for a volunteer team. 2. Keep one platform: still owned a relay and store review cycles. 3. Retire both and invest in the desktop engine: chosen. ## Decision Retire the native apps; keep a read-only web gallery for sharing. Direct users to the desktop import flow. ## Consequences - Mobile sync reliability issues end; community reaction was mixed. - The relay service was shut down in September 2025.

candidates.title: 2025-11 Sync storm
candidates.snippet: # 2025-11 Sync storm Date: November 2025. Severity: high. Owner: Jonas Weber. ## Summary A relay outage caused clients to retry aggressively. Retries amplified into a request storm when devices reconnected together, and some clients spun for hours. ## Timeline - Nov 3: relay rate limits began returning 429s. - Nov 4: retry storm; battery drain reports from users. - Nov 5: workaround published (disable relay sync); fix landed with exponential backoff and jitter. ## Root cause Retry logic had no backoff and no cap; reconnection was synchronized across devices. ## Follow-ups - Backoff and a retry budget shipped in v0.4.1. - Mobile clients were retired the following year (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]).

candidates.title: Sync Engine
candidates.snippet: # Sync Engine The sync engine moves a photo library between a user's devices without a server. Every device keeps a full local index; changes propagate as operation logs over the local network or through a user-provided shared folder. ## How it works - Each device runs a sync agent that watches the library directory for changes. - Operations are exchanged as append-only logs and applied through the conflict resolver (see [[Conflict Resolution]]). - Sync state lives in the same SQLite database as the library index (see [[Storage Layer]]). - Mobile clients used a different relay transport and were sunset in August 2025 (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]). ## Failure modes - A retry storm against a rate-limited relay caused the November 2025 incident (see [[2025-11 Sync storm]]). - Duplicate photo imports after v0.4.2 came from the dedup hash, not the engine (see [[2026-02 Duplicate photos after 0.4.2]]). ## Relations - relates_to [[Conflict Resolution]] - relates_to [[Storage Layer]] - relates_to [[Maya Chen]] - relates_to [[Jonas Weber]]

candidates.title: 2025-11 Sync storm
candidates.snippet: # 2025-11 Sync storm Date: November 2025. Severity: high. Owner: Jonas Weber. ## Summary A relay outage caused clients to retry aggressively. Retries amplified into a request storm when devices reconnected together, and some clients spun for hours. ## Timeline - Nov 3: relay rate limits began returning 429s. - Nov 4: retry storm; battery drain reports from users. - Nov 5: workaround published (disable relay sync); fix landed with exponential backoff and jitter. ## Root cause Retry logic had no backoff and no cap; reconnection was synchronized across devices. ## Follow-ups - Backoff and a retry budget shipped in v0.4.1. - Mobile clients were retired the following year (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]).

candidates.title: Run Tidepool locally
candidates.snippet: # Run Tidepool locally Tidepool runs as a local server plus a browser UI. ## Steps 1. Install the package for your platform. 2. Run `tidepool`; it creates a library in `~/Pictures/Tidepool` (see [[Photo library format]]). 3. Open the printed localhost URL. 4. candidates.file_path: decisions/Decision - Drop the native mobile app.md
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Drop the native mobile app Status: accepted, August 2025. ## Context The two-person team maintained iOS and Android clients plus a relay service. Sync bugs on mobile consumed about half of each release cycle, and the relay added a server dependency the project did not want (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). ## Options considered 1. Keep both clients and hire: not viable for a volunteer team. 2. Keep one platform: still owned a relay and store review cycles. 3. Retire both and invest in the desktop engine: chosen. ## Decision Retire the native apps; keep a read-only web gallery for sharing. Direct users to the desktop import flow. ## Consequences - Mobile sync reliability issues end; community reaction was mixed. - The relay service was shut down in September 2025.

candidates.title: Decision - CRDT conflict resolution
candidates.snippet: # Decision - CRDT conflict resolution Status: accepted, January 2026. ## Context Two devices editing the same album before syncing produced lost edits. Timestamp ordering failed across devices with skewed clocks; a server arbiter is impossible (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]). ## Decision Use CRDTs for collaborative collections: - OR-Set for album membership and tags. - Hybrid logical clocks for scalar fields, last-writer-wins per field. - Tombstones for deletions, garbage-collected after 30 days. ## Alternatives rejected - Server arbitration: no server. - Manual conflict prompts: users found them confusing in beta. ## Consequences - Every client must upgrade together for full convergence. - Implemented in the sync engine behind a version flag (see [[Sync Engine]]).

candidates.snippet: # Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync Status: accepted, May 2025. ## Context Tidepool began as a personal library tool. Every design proposal that added a hosted component also added accounts, privacy questions, and ongoing costs. ## Decision Tidepool stores all data locally. There is no Tidepool account, no hosted sync service, and no telemetry. Device-to-device sync (see [[Sync Engine]]) is peer-to-peer or through a user-provided folder. ## Consequences - Sharing requires exporting or a self-hosted read-only gallery. - The project avoids operational costs and vendor dependencies. - Mobile clients that relied on a relay were eventually retired (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]).

candidates.snippet: # Sync Engine The sync engine moves a photo library between a user's devices without a server. Every device keeps a full local index; changes propagate as operation logs over the local network or through a user-provided shared folder. ## How it works - Each device runs a sync agent that watches the library directory for changes. - Operations are exchanged as append-only logs and applied through the conflict resolver (see [[Conflict Resolution]]). - Sync state lives in the same SQLite database as the library index (see [[Storage Layer]]). - Mobile clients used a different relay transport and were sunset in August 2025 (see [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]). ## Failure modes - A retry storm against a rate-limited relay caused the November 2025 incident (see [[2025-11 Sync storm]]). - Duplicate photo imports after v0.4.2 came from the dedup hash, not the engine (see [[2026-02 Duplicate photos after 0.4.2]]). ## Relations - relates_to [[Conflict Resolution]] - relates_to [[Storage Layer]] - relates_to [[Maya Chen]] - relates_to [[Jonas Weber]]

candidates.title: Decision - Progressive photo import
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Progressive photo import Status: accepted, October 2025. ## Context Importing a 200k-photo library in one pass held the whole manifest in memory and stalled the UI. ## Decision Stream imports in chunks of 500 files: hash, insert, and thumbnail each chunk, then release it. The manifest is a resumable journal (see [[Storage Layer]]). ## Consequences - Peak memory is flat regardless of library size. - Import can resume after a crash; partial imports are visible and repairable. - Progress reporting is chunk-granular rather than file-granular.

candidates.snippet: # Run Tidepool locally Tidepool runs as a local server plus a browser UI. ## Steps 1. Install the package for your platform. 2. Run `tidepool`; it creates a library in `~/Pictures/Tidepool` (see [[Photo library format]]). 3. Open the printed localhost URL. 4. candidates.title: Decision - SQLite over Postgres
candidates.snippet: # Decision - SQLite over Postgres Status: accepted, June 2025. ## Context The library index outgrew flat JSON files. Candidates were SQLite (embedded) and Postgres (server). ## Decision Use SQLite, one database per library. ## Rationale - Tidepool is single-user and local-first (see [[Decision - Local-first, no cloud sync]]); a server dependency contradicts the premise. - Backups are a file copy; no daemon, no ports, no credentials. - Full-text and vector search both work in-process, which keeps the sync engine simple. ## Consequences - Concurrent writers rely on WAL mode; multi-process access needs care. - Migrations run at startup and must stay backward compatible for one release.

candidates.title: Mobile App
candidates.snippet: # Mobile App Tidepool shipped iOS and Android clients from 2023 to 2025. They were retired in August 2025. ## History - The mobile clients synced through a relay service rather than peer-to-peer. - Maintenance consumed roughly half of the two-person team's release time. - The drop decision and its consequences are recorded in [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]]. - Priya Nair owned the mobile surface and the community fallout. ## What replaced it - A read-only web gallery for sharing, plus a progressive web app experiment that never shipped. - Mobile sync reliability complaints are collected in [[2025-11 Sync storm]]. ## Relations - relates_to [[Decision - Drop the native mobile app]] - relates_to [[Priya Nair]]

candidates.title: Decision - Abandon the Electron wrapper
candidates.snippet: # Decision - Abandon the Electron wrapper Status: accepted, March 2026. ## Context The desktop shell wrapped the web UI in Electron. Bundle size, native module mismatches, and predictable security review noise kept costing release time. ## Decision Remove the Electron shell. Ship the local web UI as the primary desktop experience; revisit a native shell only if a concrete use case appears. ## Alternatives - Tauri: smaller, but a second toolchain to maintain for a two-person team. - Keep Electron: rejected on maintenance cost. ## Consequences - The installer shrinks; the auto-update path is temporarily manual. - Users who expected a dock icon get a documented browser-based flow.
